extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners / applicants)
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating patent eligibility Step 2A Prong Two
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the Step 2A Prong Two analysis of the Alice/Mayo subject-matter eligibility test: determine whether a claim's additional elements integrate a recited judicial exception into a practical application so that the claim is not "directed to" the exception. Applies to abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena, and products of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of a Judicial Exception Into a Practical Application
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application when the claim as a whole applies, relies on, or uses the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim integrates the exception into a practical application, it is not "directed to" the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B, ending the eligibility analysis. If it does not, the claim is "directed to" the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis under Step 2B (to determine whether it amounts to an inventive concept). The evaluation uses the considerations listed in the MPEP; the list is not exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should (1) identify any additional elements in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s) and (2) evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all considerations will be relevant to every element or claim. The analysis is not a weighing test; it is important to evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the applicant’s invention. Claims must be examined individually—claims do not automatically stand or fall with other similar claims in the application. For multiple judicial exceptions, see MPEP § 2106.04 II.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement in functioning of a computer or other technology (Improvements consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that demonstrates an improvement in the functioning of a computer or an improvement to another technology or technical field can integrate the judicial exception into a practical application and thus not be "directed to" the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the specification to see if it provides sufficient detail that a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly state the improvement but must describe it so it would be apparent to POSITA; conclusory bare assertions of improvement are insufficient. The claim must reflect the disclosed improvement by including the components or steps that provide it (the claim need not contain the literal word "thereby increasing..." etc.). Step 2A Prong Two evaluates improvement without regard to whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional. Examples cited: Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip-synchronization), Visual Memory (enhanced memory system), Finjan (virus scanning improvements), SRI Int’l v. Cisco (network monitors/packet analysis). See MPEP § 2106.05(a) for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying or using the exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis (Treatment/prophylaxis consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that apply or use a judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition can integrate the exception into a practical application and be eligible at Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration covers limitations that treat or prevent disease or medical conditions (e.g., acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, organ transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery). The key is that the steps use the natural law/exception to safely or effectively treat the patient, rather than merely gathering diagnostic data. Vanda v. West-Ward distinguishes claims that administer therapy as part of treatment (eligible at Step 2A) from claims where administration is ancillary to diagnostics as in Mayo. See MPEP § 2106.04(d)(2) and cited case law for application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing the exception with or using it in conjunction with a particular machine or manufacture (Particular machine/manufacture consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that implements a judicial exception with, or uses the exception in conjunction with, a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim may integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim limitations tie the exception to a particular machine or manufacture in a way that meaningfully limits the exception (see MPEP § 2106.05(b)). Mere recitation of a general-purpose computer without more is likely insufficient (see non-integrating considerations). Specificity of how the machine is used can be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing (Particular transformation consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed steps or elements change an article in a meaningful way (see MPEP § 2106.05(c)). The transformation must be more than nominal or insignificant; how the limitation interacts with the judicial exception is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying or using the exception in some other meaningful way beyond linking to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the additional elements apply or use the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, the claim as a whole may integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a catch-all 'other meaningful limitations' consideration (see MPEP § 2106.05(e)). The limitation must be more than a general field-of-use or technological environment tie and must meaningfully limit the judicial exception so the claim is not just an attempt to monopolize the exception. The Office provides examples in MPEP § 2106.05(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely reciting application or using a computer is insufficient (Insufficient: 'apply it' / generic computer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely reciting the words 'apply it' (or equivalent) with the judicial exception, merely including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, or merely using a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such recitations are treated as attempts to cover the exception in generic functional terms and do not impose the meaningful limits required. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) and cases like Gottschalk v. Benson / Alice for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the extra activity is meaningful or merely post-solution activity. If it is ancillary, conventional, or merely incidental, it will not render the claim eligible (see MPEP § 2106.05(g) and Parker v. Flook example where lack of specifics led to finding additional elements insignificant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally linking the use of an exception to a technological environment is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (a field-of-use limitation) does not, by itself, integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field-of-use limitations that merely limit the exception to a technological environment without adding meaningful technical implementation are insufficient (see MPEP § 2106.05(h)). The limitation must do more than state the environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangibility/physicality is not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element or elements is not a relevant consideration in Step 2A Prong Two; physical implementation alone does not guarantee eligibility, nor does non-physicality doom eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice: a computer's mere physical existence is 'beside the point.' Physical steps (e.g., DNA amplification) are not sufficient alone to render a claim eligible (Genetic Technologies). Conversely, intangible results may still be eligible if they improve technology (Enfish, McRO). Examiners must look to how the limitation interacts with the exception, not just whether it is physical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of claim limitations is relevant to certain considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a specific way of achieving a result is not by itself a stand-alone consideration, the specificity of claim limitations is relevant to evaluating the use of a particular machine, particular transformation, and whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of disclosure of how to perform claimed steps or missing specifics can indicate that additional elements are insignificant post-solution activity (Parker v. Flook). Examine whether the claim and specification provide sufficient detail to show the claimed limitations actually effect the purported integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two excludes consideration of conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2A Prong Two, examiners should not consider whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity; all additional elements should be given weight whether or not conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An element that is conventional may nevertheless integrate the judicial exception into a practical application under Step 2A. The conventionality inquiry is reserved for Step 2B. Examiners must therefore evaluate integration without referencing whether elements are routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: If no additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception, integration fails
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim contains no additional claim elements besides the judicial exception, or if the additional elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Prong Two analysis considers the claim as a whole; the absence of meaningful additional limitations means the claim is directed to the judicial exception. Examiners should consider how any additional limitations interact with the exception rather than evaluating them in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate specification and claims to ensure claim reflects disclosed improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting an improvement to technology as the basis for integration, the specification should provide sufficient details so POSITA would recognize the improvement, and the claim must include components/steps that provide that improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An asserted improvement stated only in conclusory language in the specification is insufficient. The claim does not need to recite the improvement in a particular phrase but must recite the structural or functional components that embody the improvement. See MPEP § 2106.05(a) and cited cases.
